One of the most interesting cases of wild animals living in a city are the wild dogs of Moscow. In Moscow, there are approximately 35,000 wild dogs living on the streets. Some of the dogs were born wild, while others are pets that have been abandoned by their owners. Some dogs live alone and others live in packs. In 2010, scientists studied the dogs. They found that the dogs have adapted well to urban life. They have learned that it is safer to cross the street with people. Some dogs appear to understand traffic lights.

RJ Palacio's first novel is Wonder. On her website, she explains that the idea for the book came to her after seeing a girl with facial deformities on the street one day. Wonder has been a bestseller in the United States and has already won several awards. Many schools are using it as a starting point for discussion about bullying, friendship and what it's like to be different. A film version is being made. Many, including me, are waiting to see what RJ Palacio writes next.

Chloe has two pet rats. They're not typical pets. She has lost count of times she's tried to explain to people that rats aren't dirty and they make fantastic pets if you look after them correctly. She didn't like rats either until her friend Martin showed her his pet rats. She saw how affectionate and intelligent they were.

Cape Town can be a dangerous place for baboons. Some have been injured or killed in car accidents and others have been electrocuted as they played with electric cables. Baboons are an endangered species. To save them and minimize conflicts between humans and baboons, the city council has employed a team of Baboon Monitors. The monitors' job is to chase baboons out of urban areas or catch them and release them in the countryside. This policy has had some success. However, it is proving hard to stop them from coming back to the city once they see it as a source of easy food.

This flexibility is very valuable to me because it means that I can easily take some time off when my children need me to go to their school performances or if I need to schedule an appointment with the dentist.  The downside is that without clear office hours, I tend to work well into the evening, sometimes skipping dinner to finish a task.

In response to protests, the city council decided to take more peaceful action against pigs. Instead of shooting them, they put up fences and made it illegal to feed the pigs. Time will tell if this strategy works. However, it may be a losing battle as warmer winters mean that pig numbers are greater than in the past.

By bringing people and animals together, zoos can help educate the public about conservation issues and inspire people to protect animals and their habitats. Some zoos provide a safe environment for animals which have been mistreated in circuses, or pets which have been abandoned. Zoos also carry out important research into subjects like animal behaviour and how to treat illnesses.

A different trend is springing up in opposition to consumerism – the 'buy nothing' trend. The idea originated in Canada in the early 1990s and then moved to the US, where it became a rejection of the overspending and overconsumption of Black Friday and Cyber Monday during Thanksgiving weekend. During the year, people organize various types of protests and cut up their credit cards. Throughout the year, Buy Nothing groups organize the exchange and repair of items they already own.

Is graffiti art or vandalism? This depends on your point of view. In many countries, writing or painting on public or private property is considered vandalism. Many street artists have been stopped by the police and have had to pay fines. Many city councils complain about the high cost of cleaning graffiti off buildings, buses and trains.

What does the art world think of graffiti and street art? Recently, there has been a growing recognition of its value as an art form. There have been major exhibitions of street art in galleries in Paris, London and Los Angeles. The American artist Elura Emerald organized a street art exhibition at a New York gallery in 2008. She defended street artists. She said 'artists who paint on the street are merely expressing themselves, not hurting anyone. They should be appreciated and celebrated'.

If most people have four to six dreams every night after the age of ten, that's as many as 2,000 dreams per year. By the time they reach 80 years old, the average person might have had 140,000 dreams. Even if we forget 95–99 per cent of our dreams, that's still a few thousand remembered dreams across a lifetime. It's not too difficult to believe that a dream event is followed by a real-life event that's similar to it.

It provides all the coal for the country. There used to be a thirteenth district. They rebelled against the Capitol in the past and were destroyed.

Around the 18th and 19th centuries two main ideas about dreams became popular. One was that the things we see in our dreams represent things hidden from our conscious mind. Freud believed that if we understand what dreams are telling us, we can understand our hidden feelings and the problems they cause. However, the other theory was the opposite. It said that dreams are just a collection of random activity in the brain. When we wake up, we try to make sense of these random images and feelings and put them into some sort of story.

Then, instead of just working out the meaning of your dreams, you might want to continue having some dreams that allow your subconscious to tell you what's on your mind!

People might not know they are part of the disposable clothing problem because they donate their unwanted clothes to charities. But charity shops can't sell all those unwanted clothes. 'Fast fashion' goes out of fashion as quickly as it came in. It is often too poor quality to recycle. People don't want to buy it second-hand. Huge quantities end up being thrown away. A lot of clothes that charities can't sell are sent abroad. This causes even more economic and environmental problems.

Most people believe that developing countries are in a terrible situation: suffering from incredible poverty, governed by dictators and with little hope for any meaningful change. But, surprisingly, this is far from the truth. Over the past 20 years, more than 700 million people have increased their income and come out of poverty. Many managers rely on sandwiching negative feedback between two positive comments in an attempt to encourage good performance. However, when feedback becomes such a routine, employees can start to perceive positive feedback as simply a form of sugarcoating the negatives, thus diminishing its value. In addition, as numbers of some wild species drop, there is an increased danger of populations becoming too genetically similar. Zoo-bred animals can be released into the wild to increase genetic diversity.

Psychologist and 'growth mindset' proponent Carol Dweck talked about the plasticity of the brain and the ability to develop skills and talents that we might not have been good at to start with. Many of us focus on the end result and seemingly innate talents, e.g. 'You really have an eye for details' or 'You have a real talent for organising events'. However, research suggests that by focusing on the process of how things are done – praising effort, experimentation and problem-solving strategies – we can encourage the development of new skills and the continued honing of talents.

The rover looks at the air around it every year. In 2014, it found the air contained another of the most basic organic molecules and a key ingredient of natural gas: methane. One of the characteristics of methane is that it only survives a few hundred years. This means that something, somewhere on Mars, is replenishing the supply. According to NASA, Mars emits thousands of tons of methane. The level of methane rises and falls at seasonal intervals in the year. It is almost as if the planet is breathing it.

Early in her career, the psychologist Carol Dweck of Stanford University gave a group of ten-year-olds problems that were slightly too hard for them. One group reacted positively, said they loved challenge and believed their abilities could be developed. She says they had a 'growth mindset' and are focused on what they can achieve in the future. They had a 'fixed mindset' and were unable to imagine improving. Some of these children said they might cheat in the future. Others looked for someone who had done worse than them to boost their self-esteem.

Most people believe that developing countries are in a terrible situation: suffering from incredible poverty, governed by dictators and with little hope for any meaningful change. But, surprisingly, this is far from the truth. Over the past 20 years, more than 700 million people have increased their income and come out of poverty. Additionally, six million fewer children die every year from disease, millions more girls are in school and millions of people have access to clean water.

Many managers rely on sandwiching negative feedback between two positive comments in an attempt to encourage good performance. However, when feedback becomes such a routine, employees can start to perceive positive feedback as simply a form of sugarcoating the negatives, thus diminishing its value. Instead, positive feedback should not simply be seen as something to cushion the negative. It should be delivered so as to reinforce and encourage good performance.

We need to be very cautious indeed about what we ask machines to do.

Are things getting worse every day? Is progress an impossible goal? In Enlightenment Now, Steven Pinker looks at the big picture of human progress and finds good news. We are living longer, healthier, freer and happier lives. The real problem is that the Enlightenment values of reason and science are under attack. In the 1950s, Central American commercial banana growers were facing the death of their most popular product, the Gros Michel banana, known as Big Mike. And now it's happening again to Big Mike's successor – the Cavendish. With its easily transported, thick-skinned and sweet-tasting fruit, the Gros Michel banana plant dominated the plantations of Central America. United Fruit, the main grower and exporter in South America, mass-produced its bananas in the most efficient way possible. It cloned shoots from the stems of plants instead of growing plants from seeds. It cultivated them in densely packed fields.
